findings.title: A leftover EPOCH staging file wedges a fresh data root permanently
findings.detail:
Both initialization branches of `ensure_current_epoch` publish the marker with `publish_marker_staged`, which writes `EPOCH.next.<pid>` *inside* `data_root`, fsyncs it, then renames it to `EPOCH` (epoch.rs:62 for `FreshRoot`, epoch.rs:114 for `InitializedEmpty`; the staged write is epoch.rs:202).

If the process is interrupted between the staged write and the rename - SIGKILL, OOM kill, a systemd start-timeout restart - or if `sync_all`/`rename` returns a transient error (ENOSPC, EACCES), the staged file is left behind and the marker is never published. On the next boot the gate scans the root (epoch.rs:96-109), sets `empty = false` for that single entry (epoch.rs:103), and `owned = true` because the name starts with `EPOCH.next.` (epoch.rs:107). The `if empty` initialization branch at epoch.rs:113 is therefore skipped and control falls to the refusal at epoch.rs:117.

The result is a brand-new installation that can never start, with an error telling the operator to "restore a complete epoch-3 backup including EPOCH" or "select new empty data and WAL directories" - neither of which describes what happened. Nothing in the tree ever removes a `*.next.*` staging file (`NEXT_SUFFIX` is only ever written, never swept), so the only recovery is an operator manually deleting the file. The tests at epoch.rs:315 and epoch.rs:411 actively pin this refusal for `EPOCH.next.123`, so it is the intended behaviour of the check rather than an oversight in the scan - but it is applied to trawld's own unfinished write, on a root that provably holds no data.

This is a regression against the base commit, which was self-healing in both windows: `create_fresh_root` assembled a `data.next` sibling and renamed the whole directory into place (a crash left no `data/` at all, resuming as `FreshRoot`), and `adopt_in_place` retried because `looks_like_trawl_root` only counted `wal/`, `YYYY-MM-DD` directories and `*.parquet` - a stray `EPOCH.next.<pid>` did not block adoption.

A second trigger needs no crash at all. `async_main` calls `init_tracing` before admission and the data-root gate, and that path does `create_dir_all(parent)` plus `OpenOptions::create(true).open(log_path)` for `server.log_file` (main.rs:774-782). With `server.log_file` set to a path under `[data] path`, the log file is created first, the gate then sees a nonempty markerless root, and every boot attempt refuses - the base adopted the root in place and started. `Config::warnings()` does not flag this placement.

Suggested fix: ignore (or unlink) entries matching the gate's own `EPOCH.next.*` staging prefix when computing `empty`, so an unfinished publish is retried instead of being read as foreign occupancy. Keeping them in `owned` for the query-only archive decision is still correct; it is only the emptiness test that must not count trawld's own half-written marker.

findings.title: #[sqlx::test] provisions cluster-global, deterministically-named databases, defeating the per-run (CI) and per-worktree (local) DB isolation this repo relies on
findings.detail:
These three tests are the first use of `#[sqlx::test]` in the workspace. sqlx 0.9 derives the disposable database name purely from the test path — `Postgres::db_name()` in sqlx-core-0.9.0/src/testing/mod.rs is `sha512(args.test_path)` → `_sqlx_test_<hash>` — and creates it on the server named by the *master* `DATABASE_URL` (sqlx-postgres-0.9.0/src/testing/mod.rs::test_context). The name therefore does NOT vary with the master database, only with the test path.

That collides with both isolation schemes this repo deliberately maintains:
- CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml): every run gets its own `coastwatch_test_${GITHUB_RUN_ID}_${GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT}` database precisely because "concurrent runs (PRs and main pushes share one CNPG cluster)" and the previous shared-database reset "raced catastrophically under concurrency". The per-run database isolates the *master*, but `_sqlx_test_<hash>` is created on the shared cluster under the same name for every concurrent run.
- Local (AGENTS.md): "per-worktree DB isolation (`coastwatch_test_<slug>`)". Two worktrees running `cargo nextest run` against the same local Postgres produce identical `_sqlx_test_<hash>` names.

`test_context` calls `do_cleanup` *before* creating, which issues `drop database if exists "_sqlx_test_<hash>"` unconditionally — it does not consult the bookkeeping table. So with two concurrent runs: the second run either (a) fails the DROP because the first run holds connections (SQLSTATE 55006), which surfaces as `Err` from `test_context` and panics at `.expect("failed to connect to setup test database")`, or (b) succeeds in dropping the database the first run is mid-test on. Either way one run fails spuriously, and (b) is exactly the cross-run destruction the per-run-database change was introduced to stop.

Secondary leak: sqlx records test databases in `_sqlx_test.databases` inside the master. CI drops the master (`drop per-run test database`), so `cleanup_test_dbs` can never reclaim a `_sqlx_test_*` database left behind by a failing run; the AGENTS.md worktree-teardown recipe drops only `coastwatch_test_<slug>` and misses them too.

Also note these fleet-schema tests provision on the *coastwatch* cluster (`config()` builds `fleet_url` by rewriting the app `DATABASE_URL`), so they do not use the fresh per-job Fleet service container that commit dac5c09 added — which is the natural place to put them. Fix direction: create the disposable Fleet databases explicitly with a run/worktree-unique name (the `TestDb::connect_or_bootstrap` idiom already in crates/test-support/src/db.rs) against `FLEET_DATABASE_URL`, rather than relying on sqlx's path-hashed global names.

findings.title: Session origin guard is narrowed to unsafe methods only, diverging from Trawl's session contract; README overstates the sibling-origin protection
findings.detail:
`require_session_origin` short-circuits on `request.method().is_safe()`, so `check_origin` never runs for GET/HEAD on any cookie-authenticated route. The sibling Fleet consumer enforces the same allowlist on *every* cookie-authenticated request regardless of method: crates/trawl-web/src/middleware/session_extractor.rs:98 calls `fleet_auth::check_origin(&parts.headers, state.public_origins(), "session")` as the first statement of `session_from_parts`, before any cookie state is read. Two apps sharing one keystore, one cookie domain (`.fleet.home.lan` in the prod tier) and one ADR-0016 contract now apply two different policies.

The README text that accompanies the change is inaccurate on this point. README.md:62 says "safe methods and callers without `Origin` retain Fleet's existing policy." That is true for the no-`Origin` case (fleet_auth::check_origin returns Ok on an absent header), but it is not true for safe methods — Fleet's existing policy there is to check, and coastwatch skips the check entirely. README.md:64 then claims "This also blocks a sibling origin on the same site, where `SameSite` cookies can still be sent", which only holds for mutations; a same-site sibling origin's credentialed `fetch` GET to `/api/documents`, `/api/editions/{id}` or `/uploads/{id}` is admitted here and refused by Trawl. Response bodies remain unreadable cross-origin absent a CORS layer, so the practical exposure is limited to side effects and cost, not disclosure — but the divergence and the doc claim should be reconciled deliberately (either widen the guard to all methods to match Trawl, or state the narrowing and its rationale rather than attributing it to Fleet's policy). The new test `session_origin_policy_preserves_missing_origin_and_safe_requests` pins the narrowed behaviour, so this will not be caught later.

findings.title: Unconditional validate_schema plus force-disabled auto_migrate makes coastwatch-web unbootable in prod whenever the shared Fleet DB drifts from the pinned fleet-auth revision, with no in-app remedy
findings.detail:
`validate_schema` now runs on every startup path, and `check_history(require_current = true)` (trawl crates/fleet-auth/src/migrations.rs:162-172) rejects in both directions: a version in the ledger that coastwatch's embedded `MIGRATOR` does not know becomes `MigrateError::VersionMissing`, and a version coastwatch knows that the ledger lacks becomes `SchemaError::PendingMigration`.

The Fleet keystore is shared with trawl-web (config/coastwatch.toml:842 points the prod tier at `fleet_prod`, same cluster as trawl's). Under ADR-0038 prod runs `COASTWATCH_SECRET_MODE=external`, and crates/config/src/lib.rs:2810 forces `auto_migrate: false` in external mode regardless of the TOML — so the `[env.prod] auto_migrate` knob is inert and coastwatch-web has no way to reconcile the schema itself. Consequence: the moment Trawl applies a forward fleet-auth migration to the shared keystore, coastwatch-web refuses to start on its next restart until TRAWL_REV is bumped and it is redeployed; conversely a TRAWL_REV bump that adds a migration bricks coastwatch-web until someone runs `sqlx migrate run` against the Fleet database out of band.

Before this change, `auto_migrate = false` meant coastwatch-web simply did no schema work and booted. The admission gate itself is the intended design (and is documented for the fresh/pre-baseline cases), but the deployment-ordering coupling and the required out-of-band remedy are not documented anywhere in coastwatch — README.md:48-53 only covers initialization and pre-baseline refusal. At minimum the README's Fleet-authentication section should state the required operator procedure and the Trawl/Coastwatch deploy ordering; the `auto_migrate` sentence should also note that the flag has no effect under external secret mode.

findings.title: FLEET_SESSION_PUBLIC_ORIGINS is now honored in full secret mode, contradicting the documented "external mode only" contract for FLEET_SESSION_* overrides
findings.detail:
`resolve_public_origins` is called from `resolve_full_secrets` (line 2534) as well as the external Web branch, and `load()` (line 2682) explicitly validates the variable in full mode. So `FLEET_SESSION_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` is the one `FLEET_SESSION_*` variable that applies in every mode. The doc comment on `ignored_session_runtime_vars` still states the opposite: "The shared runtime overrides apply only under `COASTWATCH_SECRET_MODE=external` — unlike trawl-web, which honors them in every mode."

The operator-visible effect is a half-applied override set: in full mode an operator who exports the fleet-dev-style trio (`FLEET_SESSION_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` + `FLEET_SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN` + `FLEET_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`) gets the origin allowlist applied while the cookie scope and Secure flag are silently dropped, and `warn_ignored_session_runtime_env` prints a warning naming only the ignored two — which reads as if the whole set were ignored. Impact is limited because dev and prod both run external mode (fleet-dev.toml sets `COASTWATCH_SECRET_MODE = "external"` for the web process), but the doc comment is now wrong at a config trust boundary and should either be corrected or the variable made external-only for consistency.

findings.title: Debian crash-dump harness still builds the package with bare cargo-deb, which now fails on the unpackaged libduckdb.so
findings.detail: The split of DuckDB into a separate `trawl-runtime` package leaves the maintained end-to-end Debian harness behind. `crashdump-harness.sh` builds with plain `cargo build --release -p trawl-server ...` (line 640) and then `cargo deb -p trawl-server --no-build --no-strip` (line 654), relying on `depends = "$auto"` in crates/trawl-server/Cargo.toml:8. After this diff, `trawld`/`trawl-admin`/`fleet-admin`/`trawl-web` are dynamically linked against `libduckdb.so` (verified directly on a built artifact in this tree: `readelf -d target/bookworm/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/trawl` shows `NEEDED [libduckdb.so]` + `RUNPATH [$ORIGIN/../lib/trawl]`). cargo-deb resolves `$auto` by running `dpkg-shlibdeps`, which has no dependency information for a private, unversioned `libduckdb.so` that no Debian package owns, so it exits non-zero and cargo-deb fails; there is no `-S`/symbols wiring here like the one scripts/release/package-debian.py:22-24 sets up. Even if forced through, the resulting package would carry an rpath into `target/deb-harness/duckdb-download/...` and could not load the library on the test node. The harness header (lines 37-41) asserts its whole purpose is "to exercise the package release.yml actually builds"; that is no longer true either, because the shipped .deb is now produced by scripts/release/package-debian.py with an exact `trawl-runtime (= version)` dependency. The harness is manual (no workflow invokes it; ci.yml:79 only runs the static packaging.sh guard), so this does not turn CI red — it silently removes the only end-to-end proof of the crash-dump drop-in, sysusers/tmpfiles generation, and capability transition for the real package. Fix: have the harness build via scripts/release/build-distribution.sh and package via scripts/release/package-debian.py, installing all three .debs.

findings.title: Minidump frames inside libduckdb.so lose all symbolication because dump_syms only covers the product binaries
findings.detail: The `Dump breakpad symbols` step iterates exactly `trawld trawl trawl-admin trawl-web fleet-admin` and never runs `dump_syms` over the shipped `runtime/libduckdb.so`. Before this diff DuckDB was statically linked into `trawld` (`bundled` default, removed in crates/trawl-server/Cargo.toml and crates/trawl-engine/Cargo.toml), so DuckDB frames lived inside the module that dump_syms did process and resolved against the published `.sym`. Now `libduckdb.so` is a separate module with its own GNU build-id, and `publish-apt` (.github/workflows/release.yml:328) publishes only the product `.sym` store, so `minidump-stackwalk --symbols-url https://trawl.sh/symbols/` will report unresolved frames for every crash that happens inside the query engine — the most likely crash site for this product, and the case the whole crashdump pipeline exists to serve. The workflow comment at lines 163-164 acknowledges upstream provides no full C++ debug info, but that is not the same as publishing nothing: the official shared library has a populated `.dynsym`, and `dump_syms --store symbols/ runtime/libduckdb.so` would still yield public-symbol resolution plus a correctly keyed DEBUG_ID, which is strictly better than an unresolvable module. Relatedly, the `[profile.release]` comment at Cargo.toml:129 is now factually wrong — it still tells the reader the published .sym files are "the symbolication source for minidumps — including the statically linked libduckdb frames", which will mislead whoever triages the first production crash.

findings.title: Development and CI builds now link a libduckdb.so downloaded with no integrity check, bypassing the repo's own pinned checksums
findings.detail: `DUCKDB_DOWNLOAD_LIB = "1"` changed meaning in this diff. Its previous comment described it as a safety net that was "completely ignored when `bundled` is active"; with `bundled` removed from trawl-engine/trawl-server/trawl-cli, it is now the primary acquisition path for every ordinary `cargo build`, `cargo test`, `cargo run`, and every CI job in ci.yml. It then copies that binary into `target/<profile>/deps` and emits an rpath to it, so the unverified `.so` is executed by every test run. Previously the default build compiled DuckDB from the crates.io-checksummed vendored source, so this is a newly opened binary-ingress. Fix: have dev/CI acquire the runtime through `scripts/release/distribution.py prepare` (or check the downloaded file against duckdb-runtime.json) rather than leaving `DUCKDB_DOWNLOAD_LIB` as the default.

When an otherwise-empty owned root holds an `EPOCH.next.<pid>` regular file whose bytes are NOT a prefix of "3\n", `is_staged_epoch` correctly declines to delete it (unknown bytes in an owned-looking file are not trawld's to discard) and control falls to the refusal at epoch.rs:136. It never names the offending entry, so the operator is pointed at two heavy remedies when the actual fix is deleting one zero-value file. Reachability is narrow but non-zero: a filesystem that surfaces a non-empty, non-prefix staged file after power loss (size-0 is the common ext4 outcome and IS handled by the new prefix check), or any third party writing that name. This is the residual of the original finding: safety is fully preserved (no deletion, no mutation), recoverability is not. Suggested fix: when `staged_epochs` is non-empty, or any entry matched the `EPOCH.next.` name prefix but failed validation, append those paths to the refusal string and state that a remnant with unexpected contents must be inspected and removed by hand.

Deferring `file_log.open()` past the epoch gate makes `log_file` inside the data root a supported configuration, which the commit message and docs/src/content/docs/reference/configuration.md now advertise. Nothing validates that the path does not collide with a reserved marker name. Do not relabel an incompatible corpus by editing EPOCH" — now with a real corpus underneath, requiring a hand-edit to recover. Before this change the same config failed on the first boot (the pre-gate `create_dir_all` + open left an empty EPOCH that the gate immediately rejected), so the deferral converts fail-fast into boot-once-then-wedge-later. findings.title: Preflight container sweep still orphans the anonymous Postgres volume (`docker rm -f` without `-v`)
findings.detail:
The commit's stated goal is "remove owned crashdump database volumes at teardown", and `cleanup()` (line 346) now correctly uses `runq docker rm -fv "$id"`. But the phase-3 preflight sweep still does `docker rm -f "$stale"` with no `-v`.

That path is exactly the one that handles the leak's root cause. `cleanup()` only runs when the harness reaches its EXIT/INT/TERM trap; a SIGKILL, an OOM kill, a runner reboot, or a deliberate `--keep` run all leave `trawl-crashdump-pg` on disk with its anonymous `/var/lib/postgresql` volume intact. The *next* run then hits the preflight at line 717-723, finds the stopped container, and removes it with `rm -f`. Because the container was the only handle to an anonymous volume, the volume becomes unreferenced garbage that no label or name can find again; it survives until someone runs `docker volume prune` by hand. So the pre-existing leak remains fully reachable, and each interrupted run adds another orphan of a full Postgres data directory.

Safety of the fix is the same argument the commit already makes at line 344: `$PG`/`$NODE` are fixed harness-owned names (lines 67-68), the sweep already refuses to touch a RUNNING container (line 719), and `docker rm -v` never removes named volumes, so `CARGO_VOLUME` (`trawl-crashdump-cargo-registry`) is unaffected. Adding `-v` here is strictly non-destructive relative to the `rm -f` already being performed — the container is destroyed either way; `-v` only decides whether its private data volume is reclaimed or leaked.

The operator-facing `die` message on line 719 ("Remove it with 'docker rm -f $stale' once you are sure nothing is using it.") gives the same lossy advice and should say `docker rm -fv` for consistency with the new teardown.

Secondary note: nothing in the harness asserts volume absence after teardown, so the author's reported "volume absence" check is an out-of-band evidence run rather than a committed regression guard — a future regression on either removal path would be silent.

My confirmation that /tmp is container-local is static: it follows from the packager's mount list containing no /tmp bind and no --tmpfs, plus --rm discarding the writable layer. No automated assertion enforces that invariant, so a future added /tmp mount would weaken it silently; I am not requesting such a guard for a one-line test-harness flag. /tmp writability for the non-root --user relies on the pinned rust:1.98-trixie image's standard 1777 /tmp, which I did not inspect in the image itself. cargo-deb's own temp staging under CARGO_TARGET_DIR is pre-existing and out of scope."
